stories.headline: Mathematics has changed, and Frank Calegari wants mathematicians to act like it
stories.why_read: The clearest insider take yet on what happens to a field when AI can produce the proofs, and what people should value instead.
body: In a guest post on Terence Tao's blog, mathematician Frank Calegari calls OpenAI's October 6 release of more than 700 research papers a watershed. He doesn't hide the problems: some of the papers are atrociously written, some are wrong, and attribution was largely ignored. He quotes Hugo Duminil-Copin's complaint that his open problems were all suddenly claimed as proved, and compares the moment to the long effort behind the classification of finite simple groups.

He offers six fixes: evaluate all work as if it were AI-assisted, hire through in-person interviews, demand more from journals, teach breadth in graduate school, run better seminars, and take ownership of AI-produced results. His line for senior people is blunt: if you're stressed about being scooped by AI, you aren't being ambitious enough. Swap 'mathematicians' for 'engineers' and most of it still holds.

stories.headline: Tesla's Texas robotaxi fleet hits 1,244, just 15 behind Waymo
stories.why_read: Tesla's Texas fleet grew from 59 in June to nearly Waymo's size, and Cybercabs are now being spotted outside the Austin geofence.
body: Herbert Ong reports that Tesla registered 40 more robotaxis in Texas on November 1, for a total of 1,244, citing the Texas DMV via texasavtracker.com. That leaves it 15 short of Waymo's 1,259 in the state. The mix is 573 Cybercabs and 671 Model Ys, and Ong notes Tesla had only 59 on June 9.

Separately, Ethan McKanna says Cybercab activity has been ramping up outside the geofence over the last couple of weeks in both south and north Austin, based on camera detections from @RtaxiTracker. Abhimanyu Yadav, quoting him, reads that as a sign of another Austin geofence expansion coming. Neither post confirms a date, but more cars plus out-of-zone testing is the usual pattern before a service area grows.

stories.headline: Postgres 19 is late because LLMs keep finding old bugs
stories.why_read: A core committer's numbers show what AI bug-hunting does to a mature codebase: back-patches up more than 60% in a year.
body: Robert Haas writes that PostgreSQL 19 will likely ship in November instead of the usual mid-September to mid-October window. Between August 27 and September 15, three big features were reverted: UPDATE/DELETE FOR PORTION OF, SQL/PGQ, and MERGE/SPLIT PARTITION. Comparing April 8 to September 25 in 2025 and 2026, master commits rose from 1,037 to 1,443, and stable-branch commits from 724 to 1,169.

Back-patches are up more than 60%. REL_18 received 433 against REL_17's 248, a jump of over 74%. His explanation is that LLMs are finding bugs faster than humans can fix them, and the review work comes out of release time. For any mature codebase, that's an early look at what AI bug-hunting does to the maintainer workload.

stories.headline: 2027 racks run from 200 kW to 1 MW, and power is the constraint
stories.why_read: If you plan data center capacity, these per-rack numbers are why existing halls can't just swap in new accelerators.
body: Shay Boloor lists the per-rack power he expects in 2027: about 500 kW for Nvidia's Rubin Ultra, about 1,000 kW for AMD's MI500, about 330 kW for Amazon's Trainium4 and about 200 kW for Google's TPU v9. Traditional racks drew roughly 10 kW, so he says these need new electrical designs and liquid cooling, not just a hardware swap.

Chamath Palihapitiya makes the same point more bluntly: power is THE binding constraint in AI. He was quoting Musk's post about Colossus 2 reaching about 1.2 million Blackwells. Put the two together and rack density, not chip supply, starts to look like the real limit on how fast capacity can grow.

stories.headline: Voyager 1 reaches one light day from Earth this month
stories.why_read: A 1977 probe is about to put a full day of light travel between itself and us. That's worth a pause.
body: Tony Dunn notes that this November, Voyager 1 becomes the first spacecraft to reach one light day from Earth. A light day is the distance light covers in 24 hours, about 25.9 billion kilometers or 16.1 billion miles.

In practice, that means a command sent from Earth takes a full day to arrive, and the reply takes another day to come back. The spacecraft launched in 1977 and is still sending data from interstellar space, which makes this a good milestone for anyone who likes long-lived systems.

stories.headline: The grid's 60-second blip came from batteries all checking themselves at once
stories.why_read: A neat bit of detective work where a clock-driven default in millions of devices shows up as a grid-wide frequency signal.
body: Grid operator Tennet had noticed European grid frequency dipping every 60 seconds. A Forschungszentrum Jülich team led by Dirk Witthaut traced it to large battery storage systems that run a state-of-charge power check at the start of every minute. Measurements at 80 points on Jülich's Living Lab Energy Campus confirmed it, and the paper is in Nature Energy (DOI 10.1038/s41560-026-02144-0).

The effect shows up worldwide and adds wear to hydro turbines. In Ireland, where data centers with large batteries account for about a fifth of demand, the signal's amplitude quadrupled between 2016 and 2021. The fix is simple: randomize when the checks run. It's a good reminder that a synchronized default across many devices can show up as a system-wide effect.

stories.headline: Balestriero and LeCun turn the Platonic Representation Hypothesis into a theorem
stories.why_read: A 109M-parameter text model beats 72B LLMs at aligning with vision, and the paper argues next-token prediction is why the big ones lag.
body: Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun prove that JEPAs trained separately on different modalities learn the same embedding up to a rotation, as long as their positive pairs relate the same world states. They call two observations of one scene 'good views' and corruptions of one observation 'bad views', and show that next-token prediction is effectively a bad-view JEPA, which they say explains why language models align with vision only partly and mostly through scale.

The numbers back the claim. On the original PRH benchmark, a 109M good-view text JEPA trained on the texts of 940M web images scores .184 against DINOv2, above every language model they tested, including Qwen2.5-72B at .154. On the same corpus it matches next-token prediction's alignment with 42 times fewer samples. They also build an image captioner where the only part fitted on image-caption pairs is a single rotation.

stories.headline: Leaks point to a crowded November of frontier model releases
stories.why_read: If you're choosing models for your bots, watch this week. Just treat every name below as rumor until a lab ships it.
body: X's news summary collects the signs: a 'gpt-6.2-astra' string reportedly appearing in OpenAI analytics for some users at around 20% of traffic, and 'Claude Mythos 5.5' strings on Anthropic's site describing cybersecurity and biology uses. Google already launched Gemini 4 Carbon last month.
None of it is confirmed, and the summary says so. A related X News story is about the same expected wave of upgrades. It's worth knowing before you lock in defaults on Claude Code or Codex this week.

stories.headline: Trigger.dev says an attacker read environment variables for some customers
stories.why_read: If you run jobs on Trigger.dev, rotate the secrets you keep in its env vars today. Don't wait for the follow-up.
body: Trigger.dev CTO Eric Allam disclosed that an attacker gained access to environment variables for a subset of organizations on the platform. The company says it has blocked the exploit and emailed the owners of affected accounts.

The disclosure is brief. Environment variables are where API keys and database credentials usually live, so the safe assumption is that anything stored there could be exposed. Rotate those keys rather than waiting for a full root-cause write-up.

stories.headline: Hackers set supermarket freezers to 50°C across Belgium and Sweden
stories.why_read: A clear real-world example of what happens when building controls sit on a reachable network.
body: The BBC reports that about 40 Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were hit, along with ICA and Coop stores in Sweden (seven of Coop's 800) and 13 SuperValu stores in Ireland. In one store, the freezers were set to 50°C. Carrefour said 15 of its Belgian stores were affected.

It follows a similar attack on French supermarkets last month. Whatever the entry point turns out to be, it's a clear case of building and refrigeration controls becoming a network attack surface with real costs.

stories.headline: China's first frontier AI export controls cover weights, agents and chips
stories.why_read: If anyone at work self-hosts a Chinese model, this is the part of the rule that affects you.
body: A Cloud Security Alliance research note explains MOFCOM/MOST Announcement No. 48, issued October 16. It covers 40 technologies, 23 of them AI, and an interim pre-export registration requirement is already in effect. Models are covered if they meet any one of three tests: at least 10^26 training FLOPs, at least 2 trillion parameters, or a global top-10 ranking. Agent systems are restricted at thresholds such as chains of 20 or more steps, 60 or more concurrent agents, or 200 or more tools.

The key line is service versus custody. Using a model through an API or SaaS isn't an export, but deploying it locally outside China is. Open-source models that are already public are excluded. Comments close November 15.

stories.headline: Opus plans, Sonnet builds, Haiku scouts: a Claude Code setup making the rounds
stories.why_read: You just set up Claude Code on the box. Here's the config people are trading to make usage limits go further.
body: damkin posted a Claude Code settings.json with model set to 'opusplan', Opus as the advisor model, a default effort of medium, Opus 5.5 on high and Sonnet 5.5 on medium, and CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL set to Haiku. It also defines two agents: a Haiku 'scout' and an Opus 'critic'.

Your timeline also had Tyler's tip to set Opus 5.5 to medium for unlimited Claude usage, and Neelesh's note about Karpathy running Opus 5.5 on medium. The common thread is to save the expensive reasoning for planning and review, and let cheaper models do the searching.

stories.headline: dax: hex was fully vibe coded, and it's still good software
stories.why_read: A working data point from the OpenCode team on where human effort goes once the code is AI-written.
body: dax says hex was fully vibe coded: the app, the landing page, the animations, even AI-generated sound effects. Issues get fixed by opencode, and he points out it isn't an Electron app.
In a separate post you bookmarked, he pushes back on applying 'pre-AI style opinions on programming' to this new way of working. You don't have to agree to find it a useful lens for code reviews.

stories.headline: Peter Yang's current winners: ChatGPT and Codex, Claude, Grok Bot
stories.why_read: A short, opinionated map that roughly matches how your own bot fleet is split.
body: Peter Yang's current split: browser and computer use go to ChatGPT plus Codex, design, video and 'taste' go to Claude, and 24/7 agents and scheduled jobs go to Grok Bot.
He also calls Gemini underrated for writing. It's one person's view, but it reflects the multi-tool setup a lot of builders have landed on.

stories.headline: Grok Bot weekly limits tighten as costs outrun revenue
stories.why_read: This directly affects how far your scheduled bot routines can go each week.
body: X's news summary says Elon Musk tightened Grok Bot's weekly usage limits because serving costs exceed revenue, with about 800,000 paid users. Paid tiers start at $30 a month.
Agent workloads keep using compute when no one is chatting, so routine-heavy setups like yours feel limits first. Keep an eye on weekly usage if your bot routines run every day.

stories.headline: OpenAI plans a lame-duck push and rebrands data centers as 'AI compute campuses'
stories.why_read: Data center siting fights are becoming national politics, and Texas is one of the places they'll be fought.
body: X's news summary says OpenAI is preparing a policy push for the lame-duck session that starts November 9, and is calling data centers 'AI compute campuses'. Chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane is quoted.

Public opinion is a headwind: the summary cites a Gallup poll in which 71% oppose a data center nearby. Critics, including Eric S. Raymond, are pushing back. Texas is one of the states where this siting fight is likely to play out.

stories.headline: Four AI labs agree on one robots.txt line to opt out of training
stories.why_read: If you run sites like indrayam.com, there's now a single opt-out token to decide on.
body: Per X's news summary, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic agreed around October 30 on a shared robots.txt token, __usage_ai-training, that lets site owners opt out of AI training.
Microsoft will start honoring it in February 2027 and Google sometime in 2027. If you run sites like indrayam.com, it's a single line to decide on.

stories.headline: At a White House medals event, tech CEOs swapped jokes about GPU shortages
stories.why_read: A lighter look at how scarce compute has become, even for the people who make it.
body: X's news summary describes a medal ceremony hosted by Michael Kratsios, attended by Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, Sergey Brin, Satya Nadella, Lisa Su and Michael Dell. Musk joked that a Delta flight with no Wi-Fi is the best AI sandbox.
Greg Brockman was reportedly teased for asking the group for GPUs. The account was reported by Colossus and passed along through X summaries, so read it as color, not a transcript.

stories.headline: Harness engineering is replacing prompt tweaking for reliable agents
stories.why_read: This is the same pattern your fleet runs on: tools, checks, memory and approval gates around the model.
body: X's news summary describes a shift toward 'harness engineering', meaning the tools, checks and structure built around a model rather than prompt tweaks alone. It spread through a 28-minute video from an Anthropic engineer and a paper analyzing eleven such systems.
One claim in the discussion is a 40% cut in task time. It's the same idea your bot fleet runs on: guardrails and verification around the model do much of the work.

stories.headline: Louisiana lines up $300B in LNG, AI data centers and a SpaceX Starbase
stories.why_read: Next door to Texas, a single state's pipeline brings together the energy, AI and space threads you follow.
body: Coastal's list, which you bookmarked, describes more than $300 billion in Louisiana projects, including a planned $100B SpaceX Starbase LA, Meta's $50B Hyperion data center (under construction), several LNG projects, and $18B from Amazon.

X's news summary adds that Starbase construction near Pecan Island starts in 2027 and that Hyperion is now over $50B at 5 GW. One state next to Texas brings together the energy, AI and space stories you follow.

stories.headline: A toy-numbers case for why Starship changes SpaceX's economics
stories.why_read: The simplest version of the Starship argument, good for explaining it to someone new.
body: James Cat lays out round numbers. If a Falcon 9 flight costs $10 and lifts 10 satellites that each earn $10 a year, you get $100 a year from a $10 launch. If a Starship flight costs $15 but carries the equivalent of 100 satellites, the same $15 yields $1,000 a year.

The figures are illustrative, not real costs, but the point is that a slightly more expensive launch with ten times the payload multiplies revenue. He applies the same logic to Starlink, direct-to-mobile and orbital AI data centers.

stories.headline: FSD avoids a head-on collision on a blind corner with two kids aboard
stories.why_read: A safety clip worth watching: the kind of edge case autonomy is supposed to handle.
body: Gary Mark shared a video of Tesla FSD avoiding a head-on collision on a blind corner in Northern California. He says two children were in the car.
One clip isn't a statistic, but sudden oncoming traffic on a blind corner is exactly where reaction time matters most. The video originally came from TeslasRUs.

stories.headline: A 15-year ADAS engineer explains the six breakthroughs FSD needed
stories.why_read: An insider explanation of why FSD looked impossible in 2016 and what changed.
body: Genma_Jp says he spent 15 years building ADAS perception systems and laughed out loud at Musk's 2016 Full Self-Driving promise. His explanation is that six breakthroughs it needed didn't exist yet.
He has now posted a video walking through those breakthroughs. It's useful technical background for the robotaxi fleet numbers in today's lead.

stories.headline: OmniDiff: a fast Rust git difftool that understands code, images, fonts and PDFs
stories.why_read: If git's 'Binary files differ' has ever annoyed you, this tool fixes it.
body: OmniDiff is an open-source content-aware difftool written in Rust. Its README says it can diff 99.95% of code changes and handles 98.8% of changes with content-specific algorithms. For code, it highlights only the parts that changed, such as `sum(numbers)` instead of the whole line, and shows moved code as moved rather than rewritten.

It also diffs pictures, fonts, archives, message catalogs and PDFs. A Font Awesome font comes out as a grid of the 20 changed glyphs, and a PDF shows the renamed box outlined on the page. It runs as git's external diff, with a two-pane terminal UI. The license is AGPL-3.0.

stories.headline: Kun Chen tried the Rex multiplexer and is sticking with herdr
stories.why_read: A clear explanation of the GUI-versus-TUI trade-off for anyone running agent sessions over SSH.
body: Kun Chen has mixed feelings about the Rex terminal multiplexer, which sits somewhere between a GUI and a TUI. He compares it with tmux, herdr and t3code.
For now he's sticking with herdr. If you run long agent sessions over SSH, his comparison is a quick way to see the trade-offs.

stories.headline: Gavin Baker: Mag 7 could reach $100T, but one or two will go extinct
stories.why_read: A bold investor thesis that places xAI among the few foundation-model survivors.
body: As relayed by stark0xbt, Gavin Baker expects the Magnificent 7 to grow from $10-12 trillion to $50-100 trillion, with one or two going extinct. His survival list is Google, Meta and xAI.
He also says 'application SaaS is done.' On AGI timelines, he's quoted as saying 'Elon says 3 years. I say 5 is safer.' This is a secondhand summary, so check the original before quoting it.

stories.headline: In mice, squeezing bones released proteins that slowed aging
stories.why_read: A surprising mechanism behind why resistance training might help you age better, though it's still mouse-only.
body: Science reports a Cell Metabolism mouse study led by Xiaochun Bai of Southern Medical University. Osteocytes sense mechanical force through PIEZO1, and deleting it shortened the mice's lives by 105.5 days. Squeezing old mice's tibias twice a week for four months extended life by nearly three months, roughly nine human years.
The team identified PEDF as one of the protective factors. Sundeep Khosla of the Mayo Clinic cautions that none of this has been shown in humans yet.

stories.headline: A 3D-printed cloak hides objects from infrared cameras from any direction
stories.why_read: Transformation thermotics made physical, with obvious uses in chip cooling.
body: University of Illinois engineers, working with Ole Sigmund at DTU, built what they call the first three-dimensional thermal invisibility cloak. It's a 3D-printed aluminum lattice filled with a rubber-like material, tuned separately along three axes so heat flows around the hidden region. To an infrared camera, the area looks as if nothing is there, while the inside stays at a stable temperature.
It worked from any heat direction and hid complex shapes, including head-like geometries. The next goal is hiding objects that generate their own heat. The paper is in Nature Communications.

stories.headline: World Bank: about 496 million Indians left poverty between 2011 and 2023
stories.why_read: One of the largest declines in poverty anywhere, and it comes with a caveat.
body: Bloomberg reports that, according to the World Bank, about 496 million people in India were lifted out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, one of the fastest declines on that measure anywhere in the world.
The World Bank also notes the gains remain uneven. It's a useful baseline to keep in mind when reading about India's infrastructure and energy buildout.

stories.headline: Chetan Bhagat to Indian parents: time to rethink 'beta engineer banega'
stories.why_read: A popular columnist questions the default engineering path for Indian kids, just as AI reshapes what engineers do.
body: Chetan Bhagat's Times of India column is titled 'Beta engineer banega? Parents, time to rethink your choices.' It pushes back on the default Indian assumption that a son should become an engineer.
It lands the same week that AI coding tools and stories like Postgres's bug flood are changing what engineering work looks like.
